item.title: Bitcoin rebounds after the Binance hack driven selloff as US-Iran deal hopes improve risk sentiment
item.description:
Bitcoin sold off sharply towards the end of last week following the news of the Binance security breach, which reportedly resulted in approximately $6.3 billion being drained from multiple wallets. The hack, described as the largest cryptocurrency heist in history, raised concerns about exchange security and potential contagion across the broader crypto ecosystem.

Although Binance pledged to cover customer losses, the uncertainty surrounding the stolen assets and the potential for further liquidations weighed heavily on sentiment. Around $1.53 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours, amplifying the initial selloff as forced liquidations accelerated the downside.

However, Bitcoin eventually rebounded as concerns surrounding the hack gradually eased. Binance's commitment to cover customer losses helped contain fears of broader contagion, while improving sentiment around US-Iran negotiations provided additional support to the crypto market. Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days strengthened hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough, reducing some of the geopolitical risk premium weighing on markets, with oil prices erasing most of last week’s gains.

Nevertheless, the macro backdrop remains challenging, with inflation risks, growth concerns, Fed rate hikes and geopolitical uncertainty continuing to limit the upside. We will likely need a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations or dovish Fed comments to change the current bearish trend. A surprising red sweep in US midterm elections could also support the cryptocurrency as markets could reprice the expected fiscal restraint. A blue sweep, on the other hand, could put further pressure on the crypto market if there’s no resolution to the Iran war.

item.title: Market outlook for the week of 2nd - 6th November
item.description:
Monday will start with manufacturing PMI data for the Eurozone, the U.K., and the U.S. while Tuesday the main highlight will be the RBA monetary policy announcement.

That same day, Switzerland will release its inflation data, while in the U.S., markets will focus on the JOLTS job openings and the Congressional elections. New Zealand will also publish employment change q/q and the unemployment rate.

Wednesday will bring services PMI data for the Eurozone, the U.K., and the U.S. while the Eurozone will also release its CPI flash estimate y/y and the U.S. will publish the ADP nonfarm employment change.

On Thursday, Japan will release its monetary policy meeting minutes, before attention shifts to the BoE monetary policy announcement. Finally, on Friday, Canada will print its employment change and the unemployment rate and the U.S. will publish the average hourly earnings m/m, nonfarm employment change, the unemployment rate, preliminary UoM consumer sentiment and preliminary UoM inflation expectations.

Several FOMC members are also expected to deliver remarks throughout the week.

In the U.S., the consensus for the ISM manufacturing PMI is 54.5 vs. the prior 54.5, while the ISM services PMI is expected at 54.9, unchanged from the previous reading.

This week’s data will be closely monitored for further signs of inflationary pressure stemming from the recent rise in commodity prices, which could translate into higher input costs.

Both manufacturing and services activity are expected to remain in expansionary territory. For manufacturing, Wells Fargo analysts have pointed out that longer supplier delivery times have significantly contributed to the ISM movement over the past 5 months.Slower supplier deliveries are generally viewed as a positive indicator, as they suggest stronger manufacturing activity and increased demand for input materials and components, putting pressure on suppliers. Much of the recent increase has been driven by the high-tech sector, although there are signs that activity is broadening across other sectors as well, as reflected in durable goods orders.

In services, analysts expect a degree of softness, with the employment component likely to weaken. Attention will be on new orders and business activity as key indicators of whether demand is beginning to lose momentum. At this week’s meeting, the RBA is expected to deliver a 25-bps rate hike, taking the cash rate to 4.85%. Inflation remains a key concern in Australia, as it continues to run above the Bank’s target.

Higher energy prices are one of the main drivers of elevated inflation and the RBA is concerned that these pressures could become entrenched in inflation expectations and influence business pricing decisions.

Recent communication from the Bank has hinted that policymakers are leaning toward a rate hike. A majority of external board members are also expected to support the move, although some dissent might exist, Westpac analysts said.

In New Zealand, the consensus for employment change q/q is 0.4% vs. the prior 0.5%, while the unemployment rate is expected to decline from 5.6% to 5.5%.

Analysts have highlighted that the expected decline in the unemployment rate might be primarily caused by rising employment outpacing population growth.

Westpac stressed that remaining labor market slack is likely to keep wage pressures contained despite ongoing cost-of-living challenges. Overall, the forecasts point to a slightly stronger labor market outlook than the RBNZ had anticipated in its September Monetary Policy Statement.

In the Eurozone, the consensus for the core CPI flash estimate y/y is 2.5% vs. the prior 2.5%, while the headline CPI flash estimate y/y is expected at 4.0% vs. the prior 2.5%.

This week’s data will be closely monitored by the ECB as it assesses its next policy move at the December meeting. Headline inflation is likely to remain above 4.0% in the coming months, largely due to higher energy prices.

The Bank will pay particular attention to core inflation and food prices for signs of second-round effects spreading beyond energy but for now, the situation appears to be under control.

At this week’s meeting, the BoE is expected to deliver a 25 bps rate hike, marking its first increase since the conflict in the Middle East began.

One of the main reasons for the expected move is the impact of higher energy prices on inflation, with headline, core, and services inflation all being elevated. This is combined with stronger-than-expected economic growth and improvements in PMI readings and employment.

The main concern is that persistently high energy costs could feed through into wages and broader price-setting. Although clear evidence of second-round inflation effects remains limited, policymakers have warned against waiting too long to respond. Wells Fargo analysts expect a further 25 bps increase in Q1 2027, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%.

In Canada, the consensus for employment change is 14.5K vs. the prior -68.3K, while the unemployment rate is expected to remain unchanged at 6.5%.

This would follow September’s surprise 68K decline, which was largely driven by public-sector job losses. Early hiring indicators point to improving labor demand, while the BoC’s latest survey shows that employment expectations remain positive. That said, trade uncertainty due to U.S. tariffs continues to limit firms’ willingness to expand their workforces.

In the U.S., the consensus for average hourly earnings m/m is 0.3% vs. the prior 0.1%, while nonfarm employment change is expected at 63K vs. the prior 29K. The unemployment rate is forecasted to remain unchanged at 4.2%.

The labor market continues to show signs of stability, with initial jobless claims remaining historically low and job openings holding broadly steady. Recent regional Fed surveys also point to modest employment growth across both manufacturing and services.

Average hourly earnings are expected to rebound by 0.3% following September’s 0.1% increase, bringing annual wage growth to 2.9%. However, subdued hiring and limited labor supply growth are likely to keep wage pressures contained. Overall, the labor market remains broadly balanced, with little indication that wage growth is adding significantly to inflationary pressures.

This article was written by Gina Constantin at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone manufacturing PMI holds up in October but rising price pressures give the ECB another headache
item.description:
• Eurozone October final manufacturing PMI 52.7 vs 52.4 prelim
  • Prior 52.9

Euro area industry activity softened slightly in October, with the headline PMI estimate touching a two-month low. The output index slumped further to 52.8 from 53.6 in September, dropping to a four-month low. Overall, it still marks a modest expansion in manufacturing conditions despite slower new order growth and increased supply-chain pressures.

The most notable drags were France and Italy, bucking the broader expansion trend across the region. Of note, both countries posted renewed deteriorations on the month.

In the case of France, domestic political uncertainty is the main drag and is biting at Europe's second-largest economy. That is a big problem that might have potential spillovers to elsewhere across the region, not just in terms of borrowing costs but also fiscal risks and uncertainty.

Circling back to the report, supply-related challenges remained at large in October, with average delivery times from vendors lengthening to the greatest degree since June. But despite shipping delays, firms were able to add to their input stocks during the latest survey period - marking the first month this has been the case since December 2022.

The other key takeaway from the report is that there was a rapid acceleration of cost pressures as input prices rose at the quickest pace since May. This was the second successive month that inflation has increased.

As such, that won't let the ECB breathe all too easily ahead of their December decision as inflation pressures continue to present policymakers with a headache amid growing risks of a wider economic slowdown in the euro area.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Market playbook: Can the RBA surprise markets again and give AUD/USD another reason to rally?
item.description:
The aussie will be hoping that Christmas will come early this year with the RBA perhaps delivering a timely present tomorrow. But with markets already well expecting a rate hike this week, will Bullock have anything left in her bag of tricks to give the aussie another leg higher?

As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 87% odds of a 25 bps rate hike tomorrow, which will take the cash rate to 4.85%. And this will follow the rate hike from September, with inflation proving to be a rather stubborn headache to deal with for policymakers.

But looking further out, traders are barely pricing in any further tightening beyond the one expected tomorrow. In fact, traders only see around 33 bps of cumulative rate hikes by June 2027 and that includes the expected move this week.

Essentially, that is signaling a one more and done move by the RBA. So, could the central bank catch traders off guard given the backdrop ahead of tomorrow?

I would argue that it's not outside of the realms of possibility as the central bank will want to retain as much flexibility and optionality as they can, as do all major central banks these days. The more hawkish scenario would be a 25 bps hike accompanied by stronger warnings on inflation and a clear indication that further tightening remains firmly on the table.

And if Bullock explicitly pushes back against expectations of an extended pause, that could force traders to rethink the rate outlook. If so, that would be the ideal recipe for another push higher in AUD/USD.

But for that, we need to see three things happen. The first being the RBA signaling that inflation remains a serious concern. That means simply acknowledging that inflation pressures are stubborn won't be enough.

Second, Bullock must challenge the idea that tomorrow's rate hike could be the last. And lastly, the RBA needs to sound sufficiently hawkish to shift the expected rate path.

It's not necessarily the hardest of hurdles to clear but to get through all of that is still rather challenging.

As for the more neutral scenario, it will just be the RBA delivering the rate hike as expected and then keeping their options open. That means Bullock reiterating that policy remains data-dependent without offering much encouragement for further tightening. And I suspect this will be the most likely outcome as she doesn't want to pre-commit to anything at this juncture.

Meanwhile, the more dovish scenario is where things could get the most uncomfortable for the aussie. Naturally, a surprise hold would be the most obvious shock. But I would say even a rate hike accompanied by softer inflation projections or hints that policy is now sufficiently restrictive could weigh on AUD/USD.

So, those are the three main scenarios to consider as we look to the decision tomorrow.

The question now isn't so much of whether the RBA chooses to raise the cash rate tomorrow. In all likelihood, they will deliver as expected. Instead, traders should be asking whether Bullock can convince markets that the tightening cycle still has another chapter to go. And that is where any real surprise opportunities will come for AUD/USD traders.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany retail sales slump in September as consumer weakness adds to ECB's headache
item.description:
• Germany September retail sales -2.0% vs +0.4% m/m expected
  • Prior +1.3%; revised to +1.2%
  • Germany September retail sales -2.3% y/y
  • Prior -0.4%; revised to -0.3%

Ouch. Death, taxes, and Germany economic data disappointing on expectations. It feels almost inevitable more often than not. That's a big miss on German retail sales with consumption activity softening across the board.

Looking at the breakdown, sales at petrol stations were down 3.4%, sales of food products down 1.4%, and non-food retail trade was down 2.4% in September compared to the month before. That is hardly a convincing sign that German households are dealing well with the growing inflation pressure that is tiding over Europe especially in the second half of the year.

The only bright spot is that perhaps with the new temporary fuel tax relief, running from October to December, that could prop up petrol station sales. So, we'll wait and see on that.

But overall, the decline across broader categories is signaling that the health of the German consumer is not doing well. Households are definitely feeling the pinch of higher price pressures and that is showing up in their spending activity/pattern.

As such, that just adds another troubling sign for the ECB as the central bank is in a tight spot to balance between flagging growth conditions and higher inflation across the euro area heading into year-end. Policymakers might still be able to get away with another rate hike in December but if the trend here keeps up, it will be tough to justify further tightening when even the largest economy in Europe might be running into trouble.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold is in trouble and things could get a whole lot uglier
item.description:
It's a rather troubling time for gold after having dropped to its lowest in over a year at the end of last week. And just when you think things couldn't get any worse for the precious metal, the technicals are now threatening to deliver another nasty surprise.

The latest selloff has dragged gold price back towards the $3,900 mark, leaving buyers in a rather difficult situation. The question now is whether this where they finally draw the line or are we about to witness a much deeper correction?

The plunge on Friday saw gold break below the $4,000 mark as broader market selling and liquidity pressures added to the pain. The modest bounce today offers some relief but I wouldn't be celebrating just yet. The weekly chart tells a much more worrying story.

Gold is now flirting with a crucial support level from the 100-week moving average (red line), seen at $3,882 currently. That is the key line in the sand on the charts, with the precious metal not having properly challenged that technical level since 2023.

That's a remarkably long time for such an important level to go untested and it speaks a lot to the bullish run we have seen in gold over the past few years.

For the better part of the last three years, gold has enjoyed the luxury of an almost relentless uptrend. Buyers have been happy to pile in on dips, with the longer-term technical picture offering plenty of reassurance. But now, that comfort is starting to disappear.

The recent sequence of lower highs is already suggesting that sellers are gaining the upper hand. And if the 100-week moving average gives way, I fear that could open the door to a much more painful correction.

The next major support region sits around $3,500, with the 200-week moving average (blue line) closer to $3,020 potentially coming into focus if selling pressure intensifies.

Now of course, a bounce from the moving average could still breathe some life into gold's battered outlook. However, buyers would ideally need to reclaim $4,000 first before turning their attention back towards $4,200 next.

But for now, I think the bigger question isn't whether gold can bounce. It is more about whether buyers can still defend the longer-term uptrend that they've grown so accustomed to. After all, even the strongest bull markets need to prove themselves every once in a while. And this is just that.

item.title: BOJ continues to reaffirm that inflation is here to stay, so what's stopping another rate hike?
item.description:
After their decision to leave interest rates unchanged at 1.25% last week, the BOJ is once again reinforcing the message that underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with its 2% target. There is a sense that it's almost as if they're trying to convince themselves that it might be finally time to do something about it.

Here are some remarks from their latest quarterly outlook report:

  • Rate hikes will likely help ease inflationary pressures, in turn supporting household consumption
  • Underlying inflation has accelerated to around 2%, gradually becoming embedded around that level in recent years
  • Real interest rates have been rising recently, particularly in the long and super-long-term segments
  • BOJ is closely scrutinising asset price movements, including stocks and foreign exchange rates, when assessing financial conditions
  • Will examine a broad range of economic data and surveys rather than relying on any single indicator to assess Japan's financial environment

And the inflation forecasts from the report certainly add weight to the argument that price pressures are mounting, similar to what they spoke of last week.

For the upcoming fiscal year 2027, core inflation is now projected at 2.6% - up from 2.4% in July. Meanwhile, "core-core" inflation (excluding both fresh food and energy) is seen at 2.7% compared with 2.6% previously. Those levels aren't quite what we would associate with an economy struggling to generate inflation.

So, what's the hold-up?

Well, the BOJ still wants to assess how previous rate hikes are filtering through financial conditions for the most part. And with longer-term real interest rates already rising, there is perhaps some justification for not rushing things.

Having said that, the central bank can't exactly afford to wait for too long either. There is a potential political risk to consider too as mentioned here.

For all the talk about inflation becoming entrenched, the BOJ will sooner or later have to deal with the fact that it is actions that speak louder than words. And that is especially the case if policymakers want to retain confidence in markets about their policy direction and conviction.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US midterms 2026: Is Trump about to lose his grip on Congress?
item.description:
I reckon that US president Trump might be in for a rude awakening after tomorrow. Or perhaps he is already aware of his current predicament, although I wouldn't put it past him to refuse to accept that reality. Either way, he's going to have to deal with the possibility that his grip on Congress could be slipping away.

As the US heads to the polls tomorrow, both the control of the House and Senate hang in the balance. And if the latest polls are anything to go by, Republicans have plenty of reasons to be nervous.

The national generic congressional ballot polls show Democrats holding a sizeable lead over Republicans as cost-of-living frustrations and dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency have weighed on sentiment. Having said that, the national polling doesn't necessarily translate neatly into congressional seats.

So, what does this mean for markets?

Let's start with a bit of backdrop. Democrats need a net gain of three seats in the House and four in the Senate to wrest control of both chambers from Republicans.

If Republicans lose the House, then Trump's legislative agenda could essentially run into a brick wall. As for Democrats, that would open the door to more investigations and tougher negotiations over government spending, taxation and funding.

But what if Democrats take both chambers? Well, that would certainly tighten the screws further especially when it comes to Trump's judicial appointments and other nominations requiring Senate confirmation.

All that being said, let's not jump the gun just yet. Even if we do get a blue sweep, there's still a catch or two.

The Senate filibuster generally requires 60 votes to end debate on most legislation, even if Democrats secure a simple majority. Things like budget reconciliation might offer some exceptions, but it isn't a free pass for everything. And Trump would still have his presidential veto, which requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override. In other words, winning Congress doesn't automatically mean getting everything your way.

Now that we have that sorted, what is the best way to go about monitoring these developments?

Let's run through a quick election night watchlist.

1. House results versus expectationsAre competitive Republican-held districts changing hands at a pace consistent with the polls, or is the national polling advantage not translating into seats? Keep a watchful eye on the likes of Pennsylvania, New York, California, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where even a handful of flips could reshape the balance of power.

2. Senate arithmeticRepublican-held seats in Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas will be among the important contests, with the likes of Alaska, Iowa, and Kansas also worth watching. Meanwhile, Democrats also need to defend seats such as Michigan.

3. Watch for prediction markets and repricing risksHow are the odds shifting for control over both chambers and are they moving substantially from pre-election levels? That will give a good reflection of overall sentiment and whether markets are responding to how things are moving when a certain outcome begins to take shape.

4. The dollar and Treasury yields responseKeep a watchful eye on how the dollar and the bond market play out, alongside Fed expectations, as traders begin to weigh the any potential impact on fiscal, inflation and/or growth implications. A reminder that if Trump loses his grip on the Senate, then confirming another Fed board member becomes much more complicated So, there's that to consider.

5. Any immediate funding and policy signalsIn that regard, just be watchful of any language from congressional leaders about the funding deadline on 11 December, future tax legislation and the debt ceiling. The current Congress will still be responsible for the upcoming funding deadline, but the election outcome could influence how both parties approach those negotiations - especially with a potentially different balance of power coming in January.

We'll dig into the individual battlegrounds in more detail later. But for now, this would be the watchlist I'll be keeping in mind in trying to assess the risk of more political gridlock in Capitol Hill.

But the fact of the matter is that no matter who wins tomorrow, Washington's fiscal headaches aren't going anywhere.

item.title: Gold’s slide to one-year low: margin calls amplified a fall driven by Fed hike bets
item.description:
If margin-call selling was a major factor on Friday, part of the decline could reverse once leveraged positions are cleared, which is why Commerzbank expects a recovery. That makes the tech sector an unusual short-term driver for gold: further AI-led equity losses could trigger more forced liquidation, while stabilisation in stocks would remove the pressure. The bigger influence is still oil. Throughout the Iran war, gold has tended to fall on escalation and rise on easing tensions, as oil feeds Fed hike expectations. Monday’s dip in crude on Qatar-brokered talks is therefore potentially supportive, while renewed attacks on Gulf shipping point the other way. US jobs data on 6 November and inflation data on 10 November will test December hike bets.

--

Earlier:

  • Gold price analysis today: Is the sharp selloff creating a buying opportunity or another trap?

---

Gold didn’t fail as a safe haven on Friday so much as get sold to pay for losses elsewhere, but the oil-driven Fed threat that has dogged it all year was still in the background.

Summary:

  • Gold fell more than 3% on Friday to its lowest level in a year, below $3,900, and is down about 30% from its record high
  • Commerzbank said the sharp fall in tech stocks may have triggered margin calls and forced selling of safe-haven assets, and expects precious metals to recover
  • Higher oil prices, firmer US inflation and rising expectations of a December Fed hike also weighed, after the Fed held rates with two officials voting to raise them
  • Earlier in the week, Commerzbank noted gold was falling even as rate expectations eased, suggesting other forces were at work
  • Commerzbank has argued gold’s link to oil and Fed expectations will keep it under pressure until the Strait of Hormuz reopens

Gold’s slump to a one-year low on Friday owed as much to the stock market as to the metal itself, with analysts pointing to forced selling as investors raised cash to cover losses in technology shares.

The metal fell more than 3% to below $3,900 an ounce, its lowest level in a year, leaving it down about 30% from its record high. The decline coincided with a sharp sell-off in tech stocks, as doubts grew over whether heavy investment in artificial intelligence will pay off.

Analysts at Commerzbank said in a note that Friday’s fall in technology stocks may have led to forced selling of safe-haven assets such as gold, as well as margin calls, Reuters and CNBC reported. The bank added that it expected precious metals to recover. When leveraged investors face margin calls, they tend to sell their most liquid holdings, and gold, after a long rally earlier in the year, was an obvious candidate.

Some commentary has gone further, arguing that the plunge had nothing to do with fundamentals. That overstates the case. Higher oil prices and firmer US inflation data strengthened expectations that rates will stay elevated, reducing the appeal of non-yielding gold. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75% to 4.00% last week, with two officials voting for an immediate increase, and markets now see a strong chance of a hike in December. Reports have treated forced selling as a likely amplifier of the decline rather than its sole cause.

Commerzbank’s own analysis adds some nuance. Earlier in the week, its analysts noted that gold had fallen back below $4,000 even as US rate expectations eased and real yields declined, and said the decline had not been triggered by a shift in rate expectations. That suggested other pressures were already at work before Friday’s tech rout.

The episode fits a broader pattern Commerzbank has highlighted since the start of the Iran war. Rather than rallying as a safe haven, gold has tended to fall when the conflict escalates and rise when tensions ease, because higher oil prices push up inflation and Fed hike expectations. In June, the bank lowered its end-2026 forecast to $4,800 from $5,000 while keeping its end-2027 target at $5,200, arguing that gold’s structural support, including rising government debt, remained intact and that a recovery depended on the oil shock easing.

The near-term path may hinge on two things: whether the tech sell-off deepens, prompting more forced liquidation, and whether progress toward reopening Hormuz eases oil prices and, with them, pressure from the Fed.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank stands alone with RBA hold call as 31 of 32 economists tip a hike
item.description:
With a hike close to fully priced, the asymmetry is clear. A hold, as Deutsche Bank expects, would likely knock the Australian dollar lower and rally short-dated government bonds, while a hike would largely confirm what markets already expect. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s surprise hold last week shows that central banks can defy near-unanimous pricing, which may make traders less complacent going into the decision. The oil call matters too: Deutsche’s view that Brent falls to $90 by early next year contrasts sharply with Goldman Sachs’ new $105 December forecast, so the outlook for fuel-driven inflation, and therefore for the RBA, depends heavily on how the Middle East plays out after the US midterms.

---

  • JPMorgan joins hike call for RBA’s November meeting, sees tightening bias persisting
  • RBA set for fifth 2026 hike to 4.85% as banks flag risk of another move in February
  • ING lifts AUD/USD target to 0.71 as it backs a 25bp RBA hike next week

---

On a day built around picking winners, Deutsche Bank has backed the outsider, betting the RBA ignores the crowd and holds rates while the oil outlook clears.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank’s Phil O’Donoghue is the only one of 32 economists in a Reuters poll forecasting the RBA will hold on Tuesday; the rest, including Australia’s big four banks, expect a quarter-point hike to 4.85%
  • Markets price around an 85% chance of a hike after September-quarter inflation came in at 3.7%
  • O’Donoghue argues inflation is tracking the RBA’s forecasts, unemployment has already risen to 4.7%, and rates are biting
  • He expects a clearer post-midterm outlook for oil by December, with Deutsche forecasting Brent at $90 by early next year
  • He urged the board to reach its own conclusion rather than follow the public “echo chamber”, pointing to the RBNZ’s surprise hold last week

Almost every economist and trader expects the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise interest rates on Melbourne Cup Day. Deutsche Bank is betting it won’t, the Australian Financial Review reported.

Of 32 economists surveyed by Reuters, 31 forecast a quarter-point increase on Tuesday that would lift the cash rate to 4.85%, its highest level in nearly two decades and the fifth hike this year. That group includes Australia’s big four banks. Markets price around an 85% chance of an increase, and many traders expect a hike before Christmas if it does not come this week. The decision is due at 2:30pm Sydney time (0330 GMT, 2230 US Eastern on Monday).

The lone dissenter among major forecasters is Phil O’Donoghue, Deutsche Bank’s chief economist for Australia, who expects the board to hold. His case is that markets are reacting to old news. Inflation picked up to an annual 3.7% in the September quarter, well above the RBA’s target, but O’Donoghue argues that the figure was in line with the central bank’s own forecasts. The RBA has warned since March that prices were running hot and has already raised rates by a full percentage point, taking them to their highest level in 15 years. Unemployment, meanwhile, has risen to 4.7%, earlier than expected.

With borrowing costs biting and the economy cooling, O’Donoghue believes the board can afford to wait for more data in December. By then, he said, there will be new information on fourth-quarter inflation and a clearer outlook for global oil prices after the US midterm elections. Deutsche Bank forecasts Brent crude falling to $90 a barrel by early next year. Fuel prices have risen about 60% since the war in the Middle East began eight months ago and have been a key driver of inflation.

O’Donoghue acknowledged that the RBA has a “free hit” to raise rates, simply because markets and the media have prepared everyone for one. But he said he hoped the board would reach its own conclusion rather than rely on the public “echo chamber”, noting that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand did exactly that last week when it held rates despite markets being fully priced for an increase.

He is not entirely alone in questioning the consensus. Another bank economist said markets had got ahead of themselves, putting the chance of a hike closer to 60% to 70%, and noted that the decision rests with a nine-member board after four hikes in eight months. Two fund managers have also tipped a pause, one citing the strength of the Australian dollar, near 70 US cents, and the other warning that inflation may have peaked and the economy risks a prolonged downturn.

The RBA has defied market expectations before. In July last year, it held rates when traders had priced a 95% chance of a cut. JPMorgan, among the many banks expecting a hike, has argued that senior officials have signalled inflation is not yet under control. Whether Tuesday brings a fifth increase or a surprise pause, the board’s guidance and its new forecasts will be closely watched for signs of how close the tightening cycle is to its peak. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman lifts December Brent forecast to $105 on Middle East and Russia supply risks
item.description:
Goldman’s upgrade reinforces the case that oil’s geopolitical premium is likely to persist even if diplomacy produces short-term relief. The bank’s view that a lasting breakthrough will be difficult runs counter to Monday’s talks-driven dip in crude, suggesting some on Wall Street see that move as fragile. Adding a standing disruption allowance to its base case also signals that sell-side forecasters are now treating supply shocks as a feature of the market, not a temporary aberration. Higher oil forecasts also carry wider implications: they add to inflation risks that have already pushed the Fed toward hikes, and that pressure has weighed on gold throughout the war. For energy equities and producer currencies, the revision supports a firmer price floor into 2027.

---

Earlier:

  • Tucker Carlson claims Trump weighing nuclear strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain

---

Goldman has stopped betting on a smooth return of Gulf supply and started budgeting for the next disruption, lifting its oil forecasts on the view that the world’s conflicts are not ending soon.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105 a barrel from $90, and set its December WTI forecast at $94
  • It lifted its 2027 average forecasts to $88 for Brent from $80, and to $78 for WTI from $73
  • The bank cited high disruption risk from the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, along with broader geopolitical fragmentation
  • Its base case now includes a 1 million barrel per day global supply disruption allowance for 2027, because the timing and location of disruptions are hard to predict
  • Goldman said markets are pricing a higher risk premium, with many traders expecting a lasting diplomatic breakthrough to be difficult

Goldman Sachs has raised its oil price forecasts for the end of this year and for 2027, arguing that conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine will keep the risk of supply disruptions high, according to reports by CNBC and Bloomberg (both gated)

The bank now expects Brent crude to reach $105 a barrel in December, up from its previous forecast of $90, with West Texas Intermediate at $94. It also lifted its 2027 average forecasts to $88 a barrel for Brent and $78 for WTI, from $80 and $73 respectively. The note was led by strategist Daan Struyven.

Central to the revision is a change in how Goldman treats risk. Because the timing and location of disruptions are nearly impossible to predict, the bank said its base case now includes a global supply disruption allowance of 1 million barrels per day in 2027. Goldman said the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, together with broader geopolitical fragmentation, create a high risk of disruption, and that markets are pricing a higher risk premium because many traders believe a lasting diplomatic breakthrough will be hard to achieve.

The upgrade marks a shift in tone from the bank’s view just a few weeks ago. In mid-October, Goldman argued that continued adaptation of Middle East supply would eventually bring crude prices down, while warning that renewed escalation posed significant upside risk. At that point it forecast December Brent at $90 and a 2027 average of $80, and estimated that spot prices contained a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel. It also noted at the time that global oil demand had fallen by 3.3 million barrels per day year on year in the third quarter.

The timing of the latest note reflects a busy period for supply risk. Over the weekend, Ukraine resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, and multiple vessels were reported struck or damaged across the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. At the same time, Iran has been discussing a Qatar-brokered plan that it says could reopen Hormuz within two days if Washington meets its conditions. That prospect weighed on crude in early Asian trade on Monday.

Goldman joins other banks that have raised oil forecasts after months of war in the Middle East. Its decision to build disruption into its base case, rather than treat it purely as an upside risk, suggests the bank sees supply shocks as an ongoing feature of the market, regardless of how individual negotiations play out. 

Just one of 10 attacks over the weekend.

item.title: Tucker Carlson claims Trump weighing nuclear strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain
item.description:
For oil, the claim matters less for its specifics than for what it says about the risk around Tuesday’s midterms. Even without the nuclear element, the confirmed reporting points to a real chance of renewed US strikes on Iran soon after the vote, with Israel reportedly pushing for immediate action. That keeps a sizeable geopolitical premium in crude, and helps explain why banks such as Goldman Sachs are building supply disruption allowances into their forecasts (more to come on this). Against that, Trump’s stated preference to let Qatar-mediated talks run and Iran’s two-day reopening plan for Hormuz offer a path to de-escalation. Traders are likely to stay highly sensitive to headlines from Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran this week, with sharp moves possible in either direction.

--

A dramatic, unverified claim from Tucker Carlson has raised the stakes in the debate over what Trump does after the midterms, but the confirmed picture is of a president weighing strikes and talks at the same time.

Summary:

  • Tucker Carlson claimed on X that Trump may be days away from a nuclear strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, under pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
  • Carlson cited an unnamed “informed observer” and said a decision could come by November 7, but also said Trump was hesitating and listening to advisers who favour a deal
  • The claim has not been independently verified; the White House said it does not comment on military plans, and Secretary of State Rubio has said no decision has been made
  • Trump said on Saturday the US still had one or two Iranian sites to deal with, including Pickaxe Mountain, which could be hit “in 10 minutes”, but that he was in no hurry
  • Axios reported Netanyahu is pushing for a strike right after Tuesday’s midterms, while Trump wants to give negotiations a chance; Iran denies nuclear activity at the site

Conservative commentator Tucker Carlson has claimed that President Donald Trump may be days away from launching a nuclear strike on Iran under pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The claim has not been independently verified, and nothing in official statements or mainstream reporting supports the suggestion that nuclear weapons are being considered.

In a post on X, Carlson said the target would be Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence believes Tehran has restarted uranium enrichment. He quoted an unnamed “informed observer” as saying that Netanyahu calls Trump about it every day, argued that no conventional weapon could destroy the site, and said Trump was likely to decide by November 7. Carlson also wrote that Trump was still hesitating and listening to Vice President JD Vance and envoy Steve Witkoff, who believe a deal with Iran is possible.

Carlson has publicly broken with Trump over the Iran war and has previously said the president should have been removed from office for threatening the use of nuclear weapons.

Some elements of the backdrop are confirmed. Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Saturday, Trump said the United States had largely destroyed Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities but still needed to deal with one or two sites, naming Pickaxe Mountain, and said this could be done in 10 minutes. He also said negotiations with Iran were going fine, though he described Tehran as unreliable, and that he was not in much of a hurry to take further action.

Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pressing for a strike immediately after Tuesday’s US midterm elections, while Trump wants to let negotiations play out for now.

A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding that Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.

Iran denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex, and its Supreme Leader has warned the United States and Israel against launching new attacks.

The claims come as diplomacy continues on a separate track. Iranian officials have been holding talks with Qatari mediators on a plan Tehran says could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington meets its conditions, while Iran’s security chief has described a recent letter from Vance as signalling a more positive US tone. Whether Trump chooses talks or strikes after the midterms is likely to shape the next phase of the conflict. 

The use of nukes is horrible to contemplate. If anyone would do it I'd say this guy ranks near the top of the list though. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Election scenarios: Morgan Stanley’s Wilson says buy midterm dip, sees S&P 500 at 8,000 after correction
item.description:
Wilson’s view gives investors a framework for Tuesday’s midterms: expect volatility first, then a buying opportunity. A pullback toward 7,100 would be a meaningful drawdown from record highs, so traders are likely to watch whether early weakness after the vote is met with dip-buying, as he expects. His comments on financing echo Bank of America’s Michael Hartnett today: hyperscalers moving between bonds and equity in response to market pricing suggests discipline rather than excess, which supports the credit side of the AI trade. The contrast he draws between quality companies that can live with 5% yields and smaller firms paying 8% to 10% to borrow also points to continued sector dispersion. Geopolitical risk, including the war in Iran, remains the wildcard in his otherwise constructive outlook.

---

Earlier:

  • ROADMAP: Morgan Stanley sees three catalysts ending the correction to ~7150, then S&P 500 to 8,000

-- Wilson’s message for the midterms is to brace for a wobble but not to waste it, with history suggesting post-election weakness has been a good time to buy.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson sees several “clearing events”, including the midterms, AI spending stress and liquidity constraints, that could take the S&P 500 down to about 7,100, roughly 9% below its record
  • He expects the index to rally to 8,000 once those events complete a correction he says has been under way beneath the surface for months
  • US stocks have risen six and 12 months after every midterm since 1950, he noted, though not always between November and year-end
  • He said a narrow Democratic win in Congress is already priced in, but a larger margin could add to regulatory and local pushback on data centres
  • Wilson isn’t yet worried about heavy equity issuance, and said Big Tech switching between debt and equity is a constructive sign

Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson expects a few bumps for US stocks around Tuesday’s midterm elections, but says investors should treat any dip as a buying opportunity, according to an interview with Bloomberg (gated).

The bank’s chief US equity strategist said several “clearing events” could pull the S&P 500 down to about 7,100, around 9% below its last record. He pointed mainly to the midterms, stress over artificial intelligence spending and liquidity constraints. Once those events finish what he describes as a correction that has been playing out beneath the surface for months, Wilson sees the index climbing to 8,000, despite uncertainty over the war in Iran. As we reported last week, Wilson has been arguing that the market’s underlying correction is well advanced.

Wilson said midterms are always a headwind, but the historical record afterwards is strong. US stocks have been higher six and 12 months after every midterm since 1950, he noted, although the November to year-end period has not always been positive, with 2018 an exception. He said this election carries an extra layer of uncertainty because President Donald Trump has signalled he plans to do something significant after the vote without saying what.

On the political outcome, Wilson said a Democratic win in the House and a narrow Senate majority are already priced in. A larger Democratic margin could be more disruptive, he said, potentially adding momentum to state and local resistance to data centre construction and to tighter regulation. He also argued that pushback against data centres may be peaking now precisely because it is a campaign issue, and could fade once candidates are in office.

Wilson said he is not yet concerned about the heavy pace of equity issuance from companies including Meta, SpaceX and Anthropic, which recently listed. He noted that capital is also being absorbed by mergers and a fast-growing economy, with nominal GDP expanding at around 7.5%, and said the issuance cycle may be close to taking a break within the next month.

In a view he acknowledged is not the consensus, Wilson said bond yields have risen this year mainly because of strong growth rather than government borrowing. With nominal growth of 7% to 8% and 10-year yields near 5%, he said the backdrop suits high-quality companies but not smaller, lower-quality firms facing borrowing costs of 8% to 10%, which explains the rotation toward quality.

Wilson also said Big Tech’s willingness to switch between debt and equity depending on market conditions is constructive, because it shows companies are responding to pricing. He said there is strong demand from investors for the 7% to 8% all-in cost of capital these companies are now paying. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tanker hit by two projectiles off Saudi coast as Gulf incidents reach 10 in three days
item.description:
The location of the latest strike matters most for oil. A tanker hit in the northern Gulf, far from Hormuz and near Saudi and Kuwaiti export routes, suggests the risk to shipping is spreading to waters that had been seen as less exposed. That is likely to push war-risk insurance premiums and freight rates higher across the Gulf, not just for strait transits, and to strengthen the supply risk premium in crude. It also sits awkwardly against this morning’s diplomacy-driven dip in prices: talk of reopening Hormuz within days is harder to price in while vessels are being struck across three bodies of water. An oil spill off Oman’s coast adds an environmental and operational risk for regional ports and loading terminals.

---

While mediators talk about reopening Hormuz in two days, the waters around it are getting more dangerous, with a tanker now hit in the northern Gulf and incidents reported from Saudi Arabia to Oman.

Summary:

  • A tanker travelling southeast through the Gulf was struck on its port side by two unknown projectiles 72 nautical miles east of Ras al Khafji, Saudi Arabia, according to UKMTO
  • All crew are accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported; vessels are advised to transit with caution
  • At least six incidents were reported on October 31, three on November 1 and one on November 2 across Hormuz, the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman
  • Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed responsibility for hitting two crude tankers it said used an unauthorised route through Hormuz with transponders switched off
  • Satellite imagery showed a laden tanker trailing oil toward Oman’s Batinah fishing coast, and a vessel off Limah, Oman, was possibly on fire

A tanker has been struck by two unknown projectiles in the northern Gulf, the latest in a rapid succession of attacks and incidents involving shipping across the region, raising fresh concerns about the safety of energy flows beyond the Strait of Hormuz.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said it had received a report of an incident 72 nautical miles east of Ras al Khafji, near Saudi Arabia’s border with Kuwait. A tanker travelling southeast through the Gulf was hit on its port side, UKMTO said. All crew were accounted for and there was no reported environmental impact. UKMTO advised vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity while authorities investigate. It did not identify the vessel or say who was responsible.

The attack is part of a wider pattern. Maritime security reports show at least six incidents on October 31, three on November 1 and one more on November 2, spread across the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. On Sunday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy claimed responsibility for hitting two crude tankers it said had used an unauthorised southern route through Hormuz with their tracking transponders switched off and had ignored radio warnings. Iranian state media had earlier described the two vessels as striking mines.

Other incidents have hit smaller vessels. A UKMTO warning on November 1 relayed a distress call from a vessel struck by an unknown projectile, which maritime security firm Vanguard identified as the tug and supply vessel Selat Storm. A further report involves the Liberia-flagged multipurpose support vessel SPM Bheem, possibly ablaze about 8 nautical miles off Limah, Oman.

There are also signs of environmental damage. Satellite radar imagery from October 31 showed a potentially disabled large tanker north of Kumzar, Oman, and another leaking vessel east of Sohar. Imagery from maritime analytics firm Windward confirmed a laden tanker trailing oil toward Oman’s Batinah coast, posing a threat to local fishing grounds through at least November 6.

The surge in incidents comes as Iran and Qatari mediators discuss a plan that Tehran says could reopen Hormuz within two days if Washington meets its conditions. The attack off Saudi Arabia suggests the risk to shipping now extends well beyond the strait itself, and that any diplomatic progress will have to contend with a fast-moving security situation at sea.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China private factory PMI at 52.0 beats forecasts, output growth fastest since April
item.description:
The beat offers some relief after Saturday’s weak official survey and may give modest support to China-sensitive assets such as the yuan, the Australian dollar and industrial metals at the start of the week. The price detail is less encouraging. Falling output and export charges driven by fierce competition point to continued disinflationary pressure from Chinese factories, which global markets could feel through cheaper goods exports. The gap between the export-tilted private survey and the broader official index also complicates Beijing’s stimulus calculations: it suggests pockets of strength in investment goods and exports even as wider activity softens. Confidence at a nine-month low is a reminder that the solid headline may not last if margins keep being squeezed.

--- China’s export-focused manufacturers had a better October than the official data suggested, producing more and selling more, but only by cutting prices to win business in an increasingly crowded market.

Summary:

  • The RatingDog China General Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, was 52.0 in October against 52.1 in September, above the 51.6 consensus
  • It was the 11th straight month above 50, the longest run of improvement since mid-2021
  • Output grew at the fastest rate since April, led by investment goods, and new orders rose solidly for a 17th month, though export order growth slowed to a three-month low
  • Output prices fell for the second time in three months and export charges dropped for the first time in nearly a year, as firms cited intense competition
  • Input cost inflation eased, purchasing rose at the fastest pace since February, and supplier delivery times shortened
  • Business confidence fell to a nine-month low on worries about input costs and competition

China’s private-sector manufacturing gauge held firmly in expansion in October, offering a brighter view of the country’s factories than official data released at the weekend, though firms had to cut prices to keep orders flowing.

The RatingDog China General Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, was 52.0, little changed from 52.1 in September and above the 51.6 median forecast in a Reuters poll. It was the 11th straight month above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction, the longest such run since mid-2021. The data were released at 0145 GMT on Monday (2045 US Eastern on Sunday).

The result contrasts with Saturday’s official manufacturing PMI from the National Bureau of Statistics, which slipped into contraction at 49.3. The RatingDog survey covers around 650 manufacturers and leans more toward export-oriented firms than the official poll, which samples more than 3,000 companies.

Output grew at the fastest pace in six months, with growth spread across consumer, intermediate and investment goods, and strongest among investment goods makers. Total new orders rose for a 17th consecutive month at a solid pace, helped by new product launches, improved production capabilities and firms’ own sales efforts. New export orders increased for a fourth month, with firms citing more work from clients in Asia, Europe and Africa, but growth eased to a three-month low.

Prices were the weak spot. Output charges fell for the second time in three months as intense competition pushed firms to discount, and export prices declined for the first time in nearly a year. Input costs kept rising, driven by metals and fuel, but at a slower pace than in September and below the year-to-date average.

Firms stepped up purchasing at the fastest rate since February and built up input stocks at the strongest pace in five months. Supplier delivery times shortened for the first time in eight months. Hiring rose only marginally, leaving backlogs of work to keep building at a steady pace.

Despite the solid activity, business confidence fell to a nine-month low, with some firms worried about elevated input prices and rising competition. RatingDog said cost pressures, price competition and subdued confidence warranted attention, though it expects the manufacturing PMI to remain in expansion in the near term. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s central bank goes daily on 1.25% overnight repo, moving to Fed-style anchor
item.description:
For China’s money markets, daily fixed-rate overnight operations should mean tighter control of short-term funding costs and less of the month-end and tax-season volatility that has periodically rattled interbank rates. The shift also changes what traders will watch: the overnight rate, not the seven-day rate, now looks set to become the signal of PBOC intent, so any future adjustment to the 1.25% level will be read as a policy move. With October PMIs in contraction and equities coming off their worst month in more than a decade, a cleaner transmission channel gives Beijing a sharper tool if it decides to lower borrowing costs. For the yuan, the change is structural rather than directional, but it modernises a framework global investors have long found opaque.

---

China is quietly swapping out the dial it uses to steer interest rates, trading a seven-day benchmark for an overnight one that brings its monetary toolkit closer to the Fed’s than ever before.

Summary:

  • The People’s Bank of China will conduct overnight reverse repo operations every working day from Monday, through a fixed-rate tender at 1.25%
  • The 1.25% rate, disclosed for the first time, is below the 1.4% seven-day reverse repo rate and broadly in line with market expectations
  • Seven-day operations move to a variable-rate tender with a fixed quantity, used mainly around tax periods and month-ends
  • Other tools previously priced off the seven-day rate will now be priced off the overnight rate, with spreads unchanged
  • Economists described the move as the clearest signal yet that China is adopting an overnight-rate system like those of major central banks

China’s central bank is changing the way it sets the price of money. From Monday, the People’s Bank of China will run overnight reverse repo operations every working day at a fixed rate of 1.25%, a step that moves it closer to making the overnight rate, rather than its long-standing seven-day benchmark, its main policy anchor, Reuters reported.

The PBOC said on Friday that the daily operations would use a fixed-rate tender based on quantity, and that the aim was to improve its management of short-term interest rates. It was the first time the bank had disclosed the overnight operating rate. At 1.25%, it sits below the 1.4% seven-day reverse repo rate and is broadly in line with market expectations and actual borrowing costs.

The change is more than technical housekeeping. For years, the seven-day rate has been the reference point for Chinese monetary policy, with a cluster of other tools priced at a spread above or below it. Those tools, including temporary repo and reverse repo operations and repo facilities for overseas central bank-type institutions, will now be priced off the overnight rate instead, with the spreads unchanged. The seven-day operations will continue, but they move to a fixed-quantity tender with multiple winning bid rates and will be used mainly around tax payment periods and month-ends.

In other words, the overnight rate is becoming the centre of gravity. One economist described Friday’s announcement as arguably the clearest signal yet that the PBOC is shifting toward an overnight-rate operating system similar to those used by the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. Another said the reform lays the groundwork for diversifying the benchmarks used to price loans and for passing broad-based rate cuts through the financial system more effectively.

As we noted earlier this month, the move had been signposted. PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng told a financial forum in October that the bank was studying a switch of its main policy rate to the overnight reverse repo rate. The overnight operations themselves only debuted in late June, so the PBOC has moved from introducing the tool to building its framework around it in about four months.

The timing is notable. China’s economy is losing momentum, with official manufacturing and services surveys both slipping into contraction in October and stocks suffering their worst month in more than a decade. A clearer, more market-based anchor gives the PBOC finer control over funding costs, and a more direct way to transmit any easing it chooses to deliver.

item.title: Oil slips as Iran says Qatar-brokered plan could reopen Hormuz in two days
item.description:
The drop reflects traders trimming some of the geopolitical premium built into crude in recent weeks rather than any change in physical supply, which remains constrained while Hormuz flows are disrupted. That makes the move vulnerable to reversal. Washington has not responded to Tehran’s terms, and several of them, including sanctions relief and recognition of Iranian-designated shipping routes, look difficult for the US to accept quickly. The weekend also brought claims of tankers striking mines in the strait, renewed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and lingering speculation about possible US strikes after Tuesday’s midterms, all of which point to supply risk. Until there is a concrete US response, oil is likely to stay headline-driven, with sharp moves in both directions.

---

Oil traders took Doha’s diplomacy as a reason to shave the war premium, but the two-day plan to reopen Hormuz still depends on Washington accepting a list of Iranian demands it has yet to answer.

Summary:

  • Brent fell around $2 a barrel in early Asian trade on Monday as Iranian and Qatari officials held a third consecutive day of talks aimed at ending the war
  • Iran’s foreign minister said Qatar persuaded Tehran to shorten its original seven-day plan to two days: US measures on day one, Hormuz reopened on day two
  • Iran’s conditions include lifting recent US sanctions, restoring June oil waivers, a reduced US military presence, recognition of new shipping routes and an end to fighting on all fronts
  • The US has not publicly responded; Secretary of State Rubio confirmed talks are ongoing but gave no timeframe, and Trump said he is not in a rush
  • Iran’s security chief described a letter from US Vice President Vance as a positive change in tone
  • OPEC+ holds December targets steady for third month as Hormuz disruption persists

Oil prices fell in early Asian trade on Monday, with Brent down around $2 a barrel, as Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported.

The focus of the discussions is a plan that Iran says could restore shipping through the strait within two days if the United States meets Tehran’s conditions. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that Qatari mediators had asked Iran to shorten its original seven-day proposal, and that the two sides had settled on a two-day timetable. Under the plan, Washington would carry out a package of measures on the first day, and Hormuz would reopen and navigation return to normal on the second.

Iran’s conditions are wide-ranging. Araghchi said they include lifting recently imposed US sanctions, reinstating oil waivers granted in June, reducing the US military presence in the region, recognising new shipping routes through the strait designated by Iran and Oman, and ending the conflict on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon. Iran has also sought the release of frozen funds, including those held in Qatar. Pakistan has been mediating alongside Qatar.

Washington has given no public response to the plan. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the Qatar-led talks were continuing but said he was not aware of a timeframe, while President Donald Trump said negotiations were going fine but that he was in no great hurry to reach a deal. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei offered a more upbeat assessment, saying a letter from Vice President JD Vance showed a markedly changed tone from Washington, which he called a very positive sign.

The diplomatic track is unfolding alongside continued tension in the strait. On Sunday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers struck mines and exploded while transiting Hormuz without Iranian authorisation, a claim that has not been independently verified. Iran has restricted passage through the waterway and attacked ships it says break those rules.

Whether the price decline holds is likely to depend on Washington’s response. Several of Iran’s demands, particularly on sanctions and the recognition of Iranian-designated shipping routes, go to the heart of the dispute, and the gap between the two sides remains wide even as mediators try to narrow it.
